1. The passive in the past Konjunktiv II
The formula: wäre + the participle of the main verb + worden. It expresses what would have happened to someone (but didn't).
Careful: “worden” (without ge-) appears only in the passive. “Er ist Fahrer geworden” = he became a tram driver; “Er ist gelobt worden” = he was praised.
2. The passive with modal verbs in the past
The formula: hätte + participle + werden + modal verb in the infinitive. The order at the end is fixed: participle – werden – modal.
Der Unfall hätte verhindert werden können.
Der Wagen hätte abgeschleppt werden müssen.
Das hätte nicht erlaubt werden dürfen.
With modal verbs the auxiliary is always “hätte”, not “wäre”: “Er hätte gerettet werden können”, not “Er wäre gerettet werden können”.

It was Thursday, the thirteenth of March two thousand and thirty-six, at eighteen minutes past two in the afternoon, when Leo Brandt was driving the M1 tram from the Eberswalder Straße stop heading north. He had been driving on the line with passengers for six months, but not yet alone: next to him in the cab, as the rules required, sat his instructor, Mr Schäfer, a quiet man with a moustache who had been driving trams for thirty years and spoke so little that Leo sometimes forgot he was there. It was a grey, windy day. There was heavy traffic on Schönhauser Allee, as always in the afternoon, and on the right-hand side, right at the next stop, a white van was parked with its hazard lights on, half on the pavement, half on the road.

Leo saw the van and thought, as he later wrote in his report, “nothing in particular”. In Berlin vans were always parked where they weren't allowed to be. He braked gently, as he had learned, because you always go more slowly at stops, and kept an eye on the right-hand side. The tram was doing twenty-eight kilometres an hour. And then, at the moment the front of the tram drew level with the van, a boy came running out from behind it, a little boy in a red jacket with a ball under his arm, straight onto the tracks, without looking left or right.

Leo didn't think. Later, when Kurt Wolff showed him the recording from the front camera, he couldn't remember making a decision. His right hand had pulled the control lever back, all the way, into emergency braking, and at the same time his foot had stamped on the bell, the loud, shrill warning bell that every Berlin tram has. The tram screeched. The magnetic track brakes dropped onto the rails and gripped, with a noise as if metal were tearing. In the passenger compartment someone screamed. The boy stopped, in the middle of the track, turned round and saw the tram coming towards him, with big, astonished eyes, the ball still under his arm.

The tram came to a stop one metre twenty centimetres in front of him. He wrote that later in his report, to the centimetre, because the police measured it. One metre twenty. The boy stood there for a moment longer, motionless. Then he dropped the ball, which rolled across the rails, and began to cry, loudly, the way children cry when they only realise afterwards that they were frightened. A woman came running from the other side of the street, shouting a name, “Jonas! Jonas!”, and snatched him up in her arms. In the cab Leo sat still holding the control lever, with both hands, and couldn't let go of it. Mr Schäfer put a hand on his shoulder. “Well done,” he said. They were the first words he had spoken that day.

In the passenger compartment two people had fallen. An older lady, who had just stood up to get off at the stop, had put her hand out as she fell and sprained her wrist. A young man with headphones, who hadn't been holding on, had fallen against a pole and had a bruise on his knee. Both were examined by the paramedics, who arrived together with the police after seven minutes. The lady refused to be taken to hospital. Instead she went to the front, to the cab, knocked on the glass, and when Leo opened the door, she just said: “Young man, I'm seventy-three. I'd rather have fallen ten more times than have that child be run over. Thank you.”

Leo wasn't allowed to drive any more that day. That was the rule after any emergency braking involving people, and he was glad, because his hands were shaking so badly that he could hardly do up his jacket. A relief driver took over the tram. Leo was taken in a service car to the depot, where Kurt Wolff was waiting for him with two cups of coffee and a laptop playing the recording from the front camera. They watched it together, three times, in slow motion. You could see the van. You could see the red jacket suddenly appear. You could see the number in the corner of the screen showing the time. Between the first frame in which the jacket could be seen and the moment the brakes gripped, there were nought point seven seconds.

“Do you know what the average reaction time is?” asked Kurt Wolff. Leo shook his head. “One second. For experienced drivers. For beginners it's more like one point two.” He pointed at the screen. “If you'd needed one point two, the tram would have gone about four metres further before the brakes gripped. Then the boy would have been hit.” Leo looked at the screen and said nothing. Kurt Wolff closed the laptop. “I'm not telling you this so you'll be proud,” he said. “I'm telling you because tonight you won't sleep and you'll keep thinking: what would have happened if. And then I want you to know: it didn't happen. Because you were there.”

On the way home, on the S-Bahn, Abena rang him. She had already heard; at the depot that kind of thing spread faster than any announcement. “How are you?” she asked, and Leo said: “Fine,” and then, after a pause: “No. Not fine.” Abena didn't say anything wise. She didn't say he was a hero or that everything was all right. She just said: “I got off at Schönhauser and had a look. The van's gone. Towed away, an hour ago. And there's a red ball at the stop that nobody's picked up. Shall I take it?” Leo had to laugh, for the first time that day, a strange, shaky laugh. “Yes,” he said. “Take it. Maybe someone will want it back.”

Then Leo wrote his report. He wrote it the way they had taught him in training, objectively, in the Präteritum, without feelings. “On 13.03.2036 at approximately 14:18, I was approaching the Milastraße stop on line M1. At the stop a van was standing in the no-stopping zone, obstructing the view of the pavement. A child ran unexpectedly from behind the vehicle onto the track. I immediately initiated emergency braking and sounded the warning bell. The vehicle came to a stop approx. 1.20 m in front of the child. Two passengers fell and were slightly injured.” At the end, after a long hesitation, he added a sentence that didn't really belong in a report: “The accident could have been prevented if the van had been towed away in time.” Kurt Wolff read the report, crossed nothing out and signed it.

In the evening Leo sat in Ludwig's kitchen with a bowl of soup Lena had brought, and ate nothing. Ludwig sat opposite him and waited. He didn't ask anything. He had heard everything from Kurt Wolff on the phone. At last Leo said, without looking up: “Kurt said it happened to you too. In nineteen seventy-four.” Ludwig nodded slowly. Then he got up, went to the old cupboard in the hall where he kept his work things, and came back with a yellowed sheet of paper, which he put on the table in front of Leo. It was a report. Typed on a typewriter, on the letterhead of the BVB, the Berlin transport company of the GDR. Dated: 2 October 1974. Signed: L. Brandt, tram driver.

Leo read the report. It was worded almost the same as his, only in an older German, with words nobody used any more today. A five-year-old girl had run onto the tracks on Greifswalder Straße from behind a coal merchant's cart. Ludwig had braked. The tram had stopped “immediately in front of the child”. The distance wasn't noted. Nobody measured back then. “How close?” Leo asked quietly. Ludwig looked at his hands. “I don't know,” he said. “I didn't look. I just closed my eyes and waited to see if I felt anything. I didn't feel anything. Then I opened my eyes, and she was standing there holding a doll in her arms.”

“And afterwards?” asked Leo. “Afterwards I didn't sleep for three nights,” said Ludwig. “Your grandmother sat beside me. Every night. She didn't say anything. She just read to me. «Emil und die Detektive», imagine that, as if I were a child. And on the fourth night I fell asleep in chapter three.” He smiled. “And on the fifth day I drove again. Greifswalder Straße. The same route. Because Ingrid said: if you don't drive now, you'll never drive again.” He pushed the bowl of soup towards Leo. “Eat,” he said. “And tomorrow you drive. Sleep here tonight, on the sofa in the living room. And if you can't sleep, knock on my door. I've still got the book.”

Leo knocked on the door at two in the morning. He hadn't meant to, but he had stared at the ceiling for three hours and seen the same nought point seven seconds again and again, the red jacket, the ball, the big eyes. Ludwig opened the door at once, as if he had been waiting behind it, in his dressing gown, with the old, well-thumbed book in his hand, its cover mended with sticky tape. They sat down in the kitchen. Ludwig put on his glasses and began to read, in his deep, calm voice, from the first chapter, and Leo listened, with his head on his arms, like a child. In the second chapter he fell asleep, at the kitchen table. Ludwig read on anyway, quietly, to the end of the chapter. Then he put a blanket over his grandson and stayed sitting there until it was light.

The next morning at six, Leo was back at the depot, in uniform, pale but on time. Mr Schäfer was already waiting at the tram. He didn't say anything, just nodded and sat down in his seat next to the cab. Leo drove the M1, the same route, along Schönhauser Allee, past the stop where the van had stood the day before. Today there was nothing there. Leo braked anyway, more slowly than necessary, and looked to the right. On the bench in the stop shelter sat a woman with a little boy in a red jacket. The boy was holding up a sheet of paper, as high as he could, as the tram went past. On it was a tram, drawn in coloured pencils, yellow, with a big smiling face in the window, and underneath, in crooked letters, it said: DANKE (thank you). Leo rang the bell. Once. And Mr Schäfer said, for the second time in two days, something that wasn't strictly necessary: “Hang the drawing up in the cab. That's allowed.”
